claim: Given only standardized, anonymized financial statements, GPT-4 predicted the direction of future earnings changes better than financial analysts.
quote: Even without narrative or industry-specific information, the LLM outperforms financial analysts in its ability to predict earnings changes directionally.

claim: The authors anonymized and standardized the statements as their guard against the model recalling firms, and report that its predictions do not come from training memory.
quote: We provide standardized and anonymous financial statements to GPT4 and instruct the model to analyze them to determine the direction of firms' future earnings.

claim: The authors state the LLM's predictions do not stem from training memory.
quote: LLM prediction does not stem from its training memory.

claim: Proposes direct tests for lookahead bias based on events assumed unpredictable from a prespecified information set, and finds such bias in earnings-call risk-factor prediction and in election prediction.
quote: Using these tests, we find evidence of lookahead bias in two applications of language models to social science: Predicting risk factors from corporate earnings calls and predicting election winners from candidate biographies.

claim: The authors discuss limitations of prompting-based fixes and recommend models pretrained only on text produced before the analysis period.
quote: The issues we raise can be addressed by using models whose pretraining data is free of survivorship bias and contains only language produced prior to the analysis period of interest

claim: Holding the model fixed (DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, two hours, headless), the harness alone determined outcome: two model-agnostic harnesses scored about half, the two lab harnesses run off their home model scored zero.
quote: The two independent, model-agnostic harnesses delivered (OpenCode 0.542, micro-cc 0.528); the two lab harnesses, away from their home model, delivered nothing (0.00 each).

claim: On a frontier model (Claude Opus 5.5) the harness differences vanish: an independent harness and Claude Code both nearly perfect at similar time and cost.
quote: On its home model Claude Code is flawless. An independent harness matches it on the same model, in the same time, for the same money: 0.9986 against 1.000, 22 against 25 minutes, $5.80 against $5.89.

claim: Evaluation uses fully deterministic grading against a hidden answer key, explicitly avoiding LLM judges and rubrics; only files in the output folder are scored.
quote: Grading is deterministic, i.e. we do not use an LLM judge or a rubric. The grader script reads only the files in /app/out

claim: The partial scores of the delivering harnesses came mostly from format, tool and classification components; the components needing exact euro figures contributed almost nothing.
quote: format, tool and register are earned by classifying documents, and classification was 90% right. The components that need exact euro figures — reconciliation, correction file, traps, together 0.40 — contributed 0.07 for OpenCode and 0.03 for micro-cc.

claim: The authors trace harness differences mainly to how much tool output is fed back into context, with lab harnesses feeding back over ten times more than independent ones.
quote: What goes back into the context. This is the biggest lever. Tool output fed back to the model over the run: micro-cc 277k characters, OpenCode 291k, Codex 3.75M, Claude Code 6.78M.
section: 5.3 Why the lab harnesses under-delivered off their home model

claim: Every result is a single run per harness; the small gap between the two delivering harnesses is within noise, and run-to-run variance is uncharacterised.
quote: One run per harness. Every number here is a single run. The 0.014 between OpenCode and micro-cc is within noise; the gap between delivering and not delivering is not, but its size is not characterised. Repeated runs and Pass^k are the obvious next step.

claim: The authors flag contamination risk because public-task answers ship in the repository; mitigation is hidden-data tool tests and regenerating tasks from new seeds.
quote: Public ground truth. The answers for the public tasks ship in the repository’s test folder: hidden from agents during a run, but public. Contamination of future models is a real risk; the hidden-data tool test and the ability to regenerate tasks from new seeds are the mitigation.

claim: Only the unsteered headless setting was measured; the setting the authors expect to matter most, an expert steering the harness live, was not, so the cheap-model scores are a floor.
quote: Headless only. We measured the lazy specialist. The setting we expect to matter most — a specialist steering the harness in a live session — is not measured, so the DeepSeek scores are a floor.

claim: Across repeated identical runs of the shipped finance agent, rubric criteria passed ranged 105-123 of 149 (about twelve points of pass rate), 15-28 criteria flipped between consecutive runs, and cost moved by up to 17%; a single score is one draw.
quote: Cells passed span 105 to 123 of 149: 18 criteria, twelve points of pass rate, with nothing changed. Between two consecutive runs 15 to 28 criteria flip. The bill moves by up to 17% (ratio of run totals 0.830 to 1.038)

claim: Of 20 failed trajectories on held-out questions, most failures were attributable to the agent's instructions (harness/policy layer) rather than the model, under a taxonomy frozen in advance.
quote: We classify 20 failed trajectories, from three runs of nine held-out questions, by the layer whose owner would remedy them, under a taxonomy frozen in advance: 13 belong to the agent’s instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model, none to its data.

claim: An automated optimization loop produced a real held-out cost reduction, but its accuracy gain on development questions shrank to a statistically unresolved gain on held-out questions.
quote: Under a cost objective its final configuration costs 0.34× the baseline on the held-out questions (95% CI [0.22, 0.58]) at accuracy within noise. Under an accuracy objective it gains 14 points on the development questions and 1.5 on the held-out ones (CI [−5.3, +7.2]).

claim: Structural harness changes (cheaper nested model, tool-use instruction) generalized to unseen questions, while case-specific prompt rules written from dev questions did not.
quote: The structural remedy, a cheaper nested model and an instruction about how to use a tool, survived questions the loop had never seen. The case-specific remedy, two paragraphs about ambiguities in particular dev questions, did not.

claim: Scoring used an LLM judge against the benchmark's verbatim rubric criteria, at temperature 0 with three votes per criterion and a numeric tolerance, reading only the final answer.
quote: We score against the benchmark’s verbatim criteria with our own judge: Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, three votes per criterion, a 0.5% tolerance on numeric matches, reading the final answer only.

claim: The judge's votes were almost always unanimous, but the authors stress this shows only internal consistency, not agreement with an external or human judge.
quote: of the three votes cast per criterion, the vote split in 4 of 1,080 test cells and 12 of 1,043 dev baseline cells. This establishes within-configuration stability, not agreement with an external or human judge.

claim: The LLM failure analyzer's diagnoses were cross-checked by blind LLM readers from three model families, who matched it about as often as they matched each other.
quote: Four blind readers from three model families, given only the traces, name the same fault as our LLM analyzer in 94% of cases, the rate at which they agree with one another (93%).

claim: Authors state the single-agent result does not prove transfer, and the validators were language models rather than financial analysts; human-analyst validation remains open.
quote: One agent shows, and does not prove, that the approach transfers. The blind readers are language models of three families, not financial analysts; the owner-of-the-remedy question for a human analyst is open.
section: 7.1 Limits, and what we do not claim

claim: The empirical study compares three AI agents (Codex, DSH, OpenClaw) on 62 investment-research tasks, yielding 186 agent-task records.
quote: In this section, we report the results of an experimental evaluation of three AI agents, namely Codex, DSH and OpenClaw, on 62 investment-research tasks, resulting in 186 agent–task records.

claim: Codex scored highest on both outcome and execution quality, but margins between agents were a few points, and DSH and OpenClaw were nearly tied on execution quality.
quote: Codex achieves the highest mean scores for both outcome quality (82.07) and execution quality (86.05), followed by DSH (78.41 and 81.90) and OpenClaw (76.00 and 81.87).

claim: Agent rankings were not uniform: which agent looks better depends on the evaluation dimension, and absolute scores vary by task type.
quote: The results therefore indicate that relative performance depends on the dimension considered, while the absolute scores also vary with the requirements of different task types.

claim: The framework scores checkable criteria with deterministic validators and interpretive criteria (arguments, evidence) with two independent rubric-guided LLM judges.
quote: Deterministic validation is used where the result can be checked against an explicit rule or reference value, whereas criteria requiring interpretation of analytical arguments or supporting evidence are assessed by two independent, rubric-guided LLM judges.

claim: The authors argue that correctness of financial information must be judged relative to its reporting period and what was available at the task's specified time (point-in-time).
quote: In addition, the correctness of financial information must be considered in relation to its reporting period and availability at the time specified by the task

claim: Human expert review changed the scores: expert-reviewed adjustments lowered final overall scores below raw automated scores for every agent.
quote: Expert-reviewed adjustments reduce the final overall scores relative to the raw scores for all three agents, with the largest difference observed for DSH.

claim: Evaluation-integrity checks found problems in a large share of records, with grading-integrity failures in nearly half; all were resolved before scores were accepted.
quote: No input-integrity failures were identified, while failures in the remaining three integrity checks were identified in 18.8%, 15.1% and 48.4% of the records, respectively. All identified failures were subsequently resolved before the corresponding assessments were accepted.

claim: The two independent LLM judges disagreed enough to trigger referral in nearly half of paired dimension-level assessments, all resolved by expert review.
quote: Of these, 236 (48.8%) were referred for further examination, while the remaining 248 (51.2%) did not require referral. Among the 236 referred assessments, 201 required review and 35 had proposed corrections. All referred assessments were subsequently resolved and accepted following expert review.

claim: A deployed multi-agent LLM equity system's strong-buy portfolio beat an equal-weight benchmark on the S&P 500 cohort and ranked above nearly all random same-sized portfolios.
quote: On the S&P 500 cohort the strong-buy portfolio delivers a +25 percentage-point compound-return advantage over the EW benchmark and ranks at the 99.7th percentile of 10,000 Monte Carlo null portfolios (p = 0.003)

claim: On the second (S&P 100) cohort the result was directionally consistent but not statistically significant, attributed to small per-date selections.
quote: the S&P 100 Monte Carlo result is consistent with S&P 500 but does not reach formal significance (p = 0.17, driven by the small ∼10-stock average selection).

claim: Evaluation used signals generated live at each date beyond the LLMs' training cut-off, which the authors present as eliminating knowledge leakage and as their primary safeguard against look-ahead bias.
quote: price data are necessarily absent from the models’ pre-training corpus, eliminating knowledge leakage as a potential source of apparent outperformance. This live-generation design is the primary safeguard against look-ahead bias
section: 2 System Overview (Live generation and data integrity)

claim: Performance is judged against market outcomes using a Monte Carlo null that matches the portfolio in everything except stock selection, not by an LLM judge or rubric.
quote: We test performance using a Monte Carlo benchmark that matches the actual portfolio on every dimension except selection: same universe, same dates, same number of holdings, same equal weighting.

claim: Embedding-based attribution (not an ablation against single agents or a raw model) indicates no single specialist agent accounts for the results; the edge is attributed to the combination of agents.
quote: No single agent accounts for either result independently; the edge appears to arise from their complementary, context-sensitive combination.

claim: The headline significant results rest on only 19 monthly observations, and the authors frame them as evidence from one live period rather than proof.
quote: The strongest statistical results in this paper—the S&P 500 Monte Carlo test (p = 0.003) and the ordinal score’s date-level IC (p = 0.024)—rest on 19 monthly observations and should be interpreted as evidence from a specific live period rather than asymptotic proof.
section: 6 Discussion and Limitations (Scope of the statistical claims)

claim: After a market-beta check, the estimated alpha is economically large but not statistically significant with 19 months of data.
quote: The below-unity portfolio beta rules out a pure high-beta explanation; the alpha is economically large but remains formally underpowered at T = 19.

claim: The authors state that whether the strong-buy outperformance persists in a sustained bear market is unknown.
quote: However, whether the outperformance persists in a sustained bear market is unknown.

claim: On 149 firm-quarters, the three leading LLM agents matched date-matched analyst consensus on median price-deflated EPS error (beating it on half of instances), while three weaker models had clearly higher error.
quote: Opus 4.6, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.4 have median PDEs of 0.113–0.131%, close to the 0.111% of consensus, and each beats consensus on 50% of instances; the other three reach 0.190–0.215% and win on 28–38%.

claim: Swapping the agent harness or raising reasoning effort barely changed EPS point-forecast error; all paired differences had confidence intervals including zero.
quote: Table 4 shows that changing either barely moves point forecast error: relative to OpenCode at the default effort, median paired PDE changes by −0.004 to +0.001 pp, and all five intervals include zero.

claim: For GPT-5.5, a minimal 'vanilla' tool-calling loop had median PDE 0.110 and a paired difference of -0.003 pp versus the OpenCode harness at default effort, with a 90% CI spanning zero.
All six models' nominal 80% prediction intervals were badly under-covered, with misses skewed above the upper bound because forecasts ran low.
quote: Across all six models, nominal 80% intervals contain reported EPS in only 37–70% of runs that return an interval, and most misses fall above the upper bound because the forecasts run low.

claim: Point-in-time handling: agents may use only documents available the day before results are released, from a fixed information environment.
quote: Each EPSBench instance asks an agent to forecast a company’s GAAP diluted EPS for one quarter, using only documents available the day before the results are released.

claim: To address memorization, the authors note which models lack disclosed knowledge cutoffs and ran a recall probe on the one released inside the evaluation window, finding no detectable recall of benchmark outcomes.
quote: Of the two that do not disclose a cutoff, GLM 4.5 Air was released before the evaluation window, whereas Qwen 3.5 was released within it. We additionally conduct a memorization test on Qwen 3.5, finding no detectable recall of benchmark outcomes under the tested protocol.
section: 4 Experimental setup (Temporal separation from training data)

claim: Each configuration was run three times per instance; the median run-to-run spread of error across an instance's three runs (0.057 pp) was used as the threshold for a meaningful error increase.
quote: we count an error increase as harmful when it exceeds 0.057 pp, the median spread of PDE across an instance’s three runs.
section: 5.4 Contributions of filings, transcripts, and news

claim: The authors caution that a confidence interval containing zero means the difference is unresolved at this sample size, not that the systems are equivalent.
quote: An interval containing zero means that the data do not resolve the difference at this sample size; it does not establish equivalence.

claim: On FrontierFinance, the agent harness rather than the model alone strongly shapes quality and efficiency: Samaya's in-house system scores 56.0% versus 49.2% for the strongest frontier model (Claude Fable 5) under an open-source harness, at about 2.2x lower cost.
quote:
we find that the tool harness, not the model alone, strongly shapes quality
and efficiency; that Samaya’s in-house system leads at 56.0%, ahead of the strongest frontier model
(Claude Fable 5, 49.2%) at roughly 2.2× lower cost

claim: Harness type is the dominant factor: the best in-house-harness system beats the best Finance Agent v2 (tool) harness system, which beats the best web-search-only system, and this ordering holds in every use case and rubric category.
quote:
The best system under the Samaya harness
outperforms the best under the Finance Agent v2 harness, which in turn outperforms the best web
search system—and this ordering holds across all six use cases and rubric categories (Figure 7).

claim: Under the minimal web-search harness (model plus its built-in web search, used as the baseline), Claude Opus 4.8 reaches only 33.0% rubric qualification overall (40.6% on must-have rubrics) at $1.47 per query.

quote:

claim: Scoring uses expert-authored binary rubrics, each judged by majority vote of three LLM judges from different providers; the authors say this trio closely matched a nine-judge committee in preliminary experiments. No human expert grades the system answers.
quote:
We score each rubric by majority vote across three independent LLM judges: GPT 5.4, Gemini 3.1
Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. We chose this ensemble to avoid single-provider bias and because their
majority votes closely matched a larger committee of nine judges in preliminary experiments.

claim: Evaluation is retrospective with dated queries: every system only gets the query date in the prompt and is asked to anchor on it, and only the in-house harness enforces that date as a hard retrieval cutoff.
quote:
For all tested systems, we provide both the query and its associated query
date as input, and prompt the system to anchor its research on that date. For Samaya’s in-house
harness, we additionally apply the query date as a retrieval cut-off for any data indexed in-house.

claim: The authors state a temporal limitation: as models are trained on data that postdates the query dates, they may answer from memory rather than through retrieval and tool use, and this risk grows over time.
quote:
As future LLMs are trained
on data postdating the query dates, they may answer from parametric knowledge rather than through
active retrieval and tool use—the very capabilities the benchmark is designed to test.

claim: In their pairwise LLM-judge difficulty ranking, swapping A/B order flipped the winner on 7% of consensus results, mostly in low-confidence calls (28%/11%/2% at margins 1/2/3).
quote:
Re-judging a fixed 20,000-pair sample with the two queries in swapped A/B order
flips the winner on 7% of consensus results, concentrated in low-confidence calls—28/11/2% at
margins 1/2/3 (Table 11).

claim: On a benchmark of whether agents can tell if news is new, important and directional for a stock, the best of 14 frontier agents matches all three expert labels on only 52.4% of cases.
quote:
The strongest agent we
evaluate on Frontier Financial Judgement matches all expert labels in only 52.4% of cases.

claim: Leakage control by design: analysts write synthetic but plausible events and mix them with real live articles, so agents can use ordinary web search with minimal risk that the answer leaks from online sources.
quote:
By combining purely synthetic events with actual articles, we allow agents to
access normal web search tools while still ensuring that there is minimal risk the correct answer will leak
from online sources [17, 32].

claim: Ground truth comes from professional analysts' gold labels, and scoring is exact match against them with no LLM judge; missing or malformed outputs count as wrong.
quote:
A prediction is counted as correct when it
matches either the primary expert label or an accepted secondary label for a genuine boundary case. Missing
or malformed outputs remain in the benchmark denominator and are counted as incorrect.

claim: The authors criticise point-in-time financial RAG benchmarks that use later realised market returns as labels, because returns mix the event's meaning with wider market conditions.
quote:
Point-in-time financial RAG is particularly relevant as it
evaluates news-triggered event-impact prediction using only contemporaneous evidence. However, it uses
subsequently realised market returns as labels, which may conflate event interpretation with wider market
conditions.

claim: Accuracy on target events does not predict false-positive behaviour: GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.8 score similarly on target events, yet Opus flags about five times more surrounding live articles (35% vs 7%).
quote:
For example, GPT-5.4
and Claude Opus 4.8 perform similarly on the target events, but Claude Opus has approximately five times
the false-positive rate on the surrounding live articles (35% versus 7%).

claim: The shared failures are numeric and contextual reasoning, not retrieval: on one case every agent followed a positive year-on-year headline instead of calculating the negative sequential revision implied by the figures and prior guidance.
quote:
In Figure 5, every agent recognises that the forecast is new, but every
agent follows its positive year-on-year headline rather than calculating the negative sequential revision
implied by the figures and prior guidance.

claim: The authors treat the whole agent configuration (model, harness, reasoning setting, prompt, tool policy) as the unit evaluated; they do not compare harness against bare model.
quote:
We treat the complete agent configuration, comprising the model, harness, reasoning configuration, prompt,
and tool policy, as the evaluated unit.

claim: Stated limitations: the first version covers only semiconductor supply-chain companies and may not generalise; some expert labels are subjective and other professionals could reasonably disagree. They also note synthetic events miss competing interpretations across articles.
quote:
This first version of Frontier Financial
Judgement focuses on semiconductor supply-chain companies, and its results may not generalise to other
sectors. Finally, some expert judgements are inherently subjective, and other financial professionals may
reasonably have assigned different labels.

claim: On the Finance Agent Benchmark (expert-written SEC-filing research questions answered by tool-using agents), the best model, o3, reached only 46.8% accuracy at an average of $3.79 per query.
quote:
Our evaluation reveals significant limitations in current AI capabilities—even the
best-performing model (OpenAI’s o3) achieved only 46.8% accuracy, at an average
cost of $3.79 per query.

claim: To limit contamination, experts wrote questions about documents published no earlier than 2024, after most training cutoffs. The questions are answerable from the open internet or public filings.
quote:
Questions were designed to be answerable without additional information beyond what is
available on the open internet or in public filings. The experts focused their question generation on
documents published no earlier than 2024 (after most training cutoffs).

claim: Answers are scored by an LLM judge against rubrics, each rubric a specific component of the expert solution, rather than holistically.
quote:
Our benchmark uses an LLM-as-judge approach
with rubric-based assessment that evaluates answers against specific components of expert solutions
rather than holistically.

claim: GPT-4o extracted the grading rubrics automatically from the expert questions and answers, and the paper's authors, not the domain experts, checked them by hand.
quote:
We used GPT-4o to automatically extract initial rubrics from the
experts’ questions and answers (see Appendix C.1 for the exact prompts used). Each question, answer,
and its associated rubrics were then manually reviewed by the authors of this paper

claim: Performance differs sharply by task type: models handle simple retrieval better than complex financial modeling or market analysis, so autonomous use in high-stakes finance is not yet reliable.
quote:
The stark performance differences across task types—with models
handling simple retrieval better than complex financial modeling or market analysis—suggests that
while AI agents show promise for automating routine financial tasks, considerable advancement is
needed

claim: Models were asked for citations or sources, but the benchmark did not check whether those sources were accurate or reliable. The authors list this as a limitation.
quote:
Moreover, although we asked models to provide citations or sources for their answers, we did
not evaluate the accuracy or reliability of these sources.

claim: Stated limitation: the evaluation harness is a simple ReAct-style loop and does not represent commercial RAG systems or proprietary agent tools.
quote:
While sufficient to evaluate
general capabilities, it is not representative of the full complexity of commercial retrieval-augmented
generation (RAG) systems or proprietary agentic tools developed by industry leaders such as OpenAI,
Google, or xAI.

claim: Against a human baseline, the most expensive model (o3) averaged 3.1 minutes and $3.78 per task versus 16.8 minutes and $25.66 for human experts. The human figures count only answering time.
quote:
even the most expensive
model (o3) averages just 3.1 minutes per task and costs $3.78, compared to human experts requiring
16.8 minutes and costing $25.66

claim: On a live weekly financial-forecasting benchmark, the deep-research agents score highest: o3-deep-research at 39.5% and Perplexity Sonar Deep Research at 39.4%, roughly level with each other.
quote:
OpenAI o3-deep-research (39.5%) and Perplexity Sonar Deep Research (39.4%) outperform all
other architectural approaches, with their near-parity suggesting convergence at the frontier of this paradigm.

claim: The benchmark is prospective (live): new tasks are released every week and scored only after the real outcome is disclosed, so the answer cannot be known at prediction time.
quote:
The benchmark has operated continuously since 27 October 2025, releasing a new task
batch every Thursday.

claim: The authors argue that existing financial forecasting benchmarks are evaluated once on historical data whose ground truth is already known at test time, which makes them inherently vulnerable to data contamination.
quote:
These are typically evaluated in a one-time setting on historical data, where the ground
truth is already known at test time, leading to inherently vulnerable to data contamination.

claim: Numeric forecasts are scored deterministically as correct or incorrect within fixed relative-error tolerances: 5% for million-scale financial metrics, 1% for percentage and ratio metrics, and 0.1% for interest and FX rates. No LLM judge is used.
quote:
By unit type, thresholds are set to 5% for million-scale financial metrics and 1% for percentage and ratio
metrics. By indicator category, thresholds are set to 0.1% for interest rates and foreign exchange rates

claim: For event (non-recurrent) tasks, ground truth is aggregated from multiple sources and verified by experts, with 95% inter-annotator agreement.
quote:
For non-recurrent tasks, ground truth is determined through evidence aggregation from
multiple sources, with expert verification achieving 95% inter-annotator agreement.

claim: The gain of a specialised deep-research agent over frontier models with built-in search is small: the best thinking+search models score 35.0–36.0%, only 3–4 points below the deep-research systems.
quote:
The leading Thinking + Search (T+S) models, GPT-5 (36.0%), Claude-Sonnet-4.5 (35.9%), and Gemini 2.5 Pro
(35.0%), cluster within a narrow band yet consistently underperform Deep Research systems by 3-4 percentage
points

claim: Within the same model, removing web search lowers accuracy by 11.0 to 14.2 percentage points (e.g., GPT-5 from 36.0% to 25.0%), so access to external information largely determines success.
quote:
Within-model
comparisons between T and T+S configurations reveal systematic accuracy degradation when search is removed,
with performance drops ranging from 11.0 percentage points (GPT-5: 36.0% →25.0%) to 14.2 percentage points
(Gemini 2.5 Pro: 35.0% →20.8%).

claim: Precise numeric forecasting (scheduled metrics such as EPS) is far harder than binary event prediction: accuracy reaches up to 81.4% on event tasks, but the best method gets only 25.5% on recurrent numeric tasks.
quote:
Across all paradigms, models
achieve high accuracy on non-recurrent tasks (up to 81.4%), while performance on recurrent tasks drops sharply,
with the best method reaching only 25.5% overall.

claim: The gold standard for evaluating a forecaster is to score it on unresolved questions after they resolve. The authors note this is impractical for rapid evaluation, so researchers fall back on backtesting.
quote:
The gold standard for evaluating a
forecaster involves running it on unresolved questions, waiting until the questions resolve, and then
scoring the predictions. However, this approach is impractical for rapid model evaluation.

claim: Logical leakage: in a backtest, the fact that a question has already resolved by the evaluation date can reveal the answer. A forecaster asked in 2025 whether Queen Elizabeth would live to 100 can deduce 'no', because a 'yes' could not resolve until 2026.
quote:
But if the forecaster knows that it is being evaluated in 2025, then it can deduce
that the correct answer cannot be “yes”, as Queen Elizabeth would have turned 100 in 2026.
section: 2.1 Issue 1: Logical Leakage of Outcomes in Backtesting

claim: Logical leakage shows up in published benchmarks: at least 3.8% of one dataset's questions had already resolved early, so no forecasting was needed, and at least 10% of another's were trivial given their resolution date.
quote:
We find that at least 3.8% of their dataset consists of questions
for events that resolved “early” and where hence no forecasting is needed. Similarly, the dataset in
Tao et al. [2025] consists of questions that resolved by August 2024, with at least 10% of questions
being trivial to forecast

claim: Questions generated after the fact from news carry survivorship bias: a company that shut down gets little later coverage, so news-generated backtest sets rarely ask about it, and the backtest question mix differs from what a live forecaster would face.
quote:
Consider a company that shuts down in Q1 2025. Post-shutdown, fewer news articles
will be written about this company, reducing the likelihood that question-generation procedures will
create backtesting questions about its 2025 outcomes.

claim: Unreliable date-restricted retrieval: a search restricted to January–September 2024 returned a page dated 14 January 2024 that already highlighted the October 2024 Nobel Peace Prize, so a backtested system could see the future.
quote:
Figure 3 in Appendix A shows an example where a search for the Nobel Peace Prize winner “Nihon
Hidankyo” restricted to January-September 2024 returns a result with a claimed publication date of
14 January 2024, yet highlighting the Nobel Prize (which was announced in October 2024).

claim: Point-in-time financial data leaks the same way: historical fundamentals can be overwritten by later restatements. Enron changed its 1998-2001 earnings in 2002, and many data repositories no longer report the original values.
quote:
Breitschwerdt [2015] highlight how Enron
drastically changed its 1998-2001 earnings in 2002, and many data repositories do not report the
original values anymore.

claim: Stated knowledge cutoffs are not guarantees: a model's real knowledge can extend a few months past the stated cutoff, so the authors recommend a few-month buffer when backtesting.
quote:
As the example in Figure 2b shows, the actual knowledge cutoff may be up to a few months after
the stated cutoff date. Thus, having a few-month buffer is prudent and might resolve this issue in
practice.
section: 2.3 Issue 3: Over-reliance on Model Cutoff Dates (Possible solutions)

claim: Benchmark gaming: betting confidently on one scenario can top a leaderboard, so when many systems with different biases are compared, the top performer is likely overestimated, ranked high through systematic overconfidence rather than skill.
quote:
This creates a winner’s curse problem: when benchmarking many LLMs with different
biases, the top performer is likely overestimated, having achieved its ranking through systematic
overconfidence rather than superior forecasting ability.

claim: LLMs cannot be trusted for forecasts of periods inside their training data: if the model saw the realized values, genuine skill and memorization are observationally equivalent, and any measured memorization is only a lower bound.
quote: Counterfactual forecasting ability is non-identified when the model has seen the realized values: any observed output is consistent with both genuine skill and memorization. Any evidence of memorization represents only a lower bound on encoded knowledge.

claim: Telling GPT-4o to ignore information after 2010 did not reduce its GDP-direction accuracy after the fake cutoff (97.6% before vs 98.0% after), whereas accuracy on truly post-knowledge-cutoff data was only 40%.
quote: the model achieves 97.6% threshold accuracy before the artificial cutoff and 98.0% after, nearly identical performance despite the explicit constraint.2 In contrast, actual post-knowledge cutoff accuracy is only 40%.

claim: When the fake 2010 cutoff was stated only in the system prompt, post-fake-cutoff GDP predictions stayed implausibly accurate (0.05% error, 98.00% accuracy) with just one refusal in 50 observations.
quote: Still, post-fake-cutoff performance remains implausibly strong (0.05% error, 98.00% accuracy) with only one refusal across 50 observations.
section: 5.5 Can LLMs Follow “Fake” Knowledge Cutoff Prompts?

claim: With the fake 2010 cutoff in both the system and user prompts, post-fake-cutoff accuracy fell (69.23%) and refusals rose (38 of 51 observations).
quote: but struggles post-fake-cutoff, showing a higher error (0.59%) and lower accuracy (69.23%), with 38 refusals out of 51 post-fake-cutoff observations.
section: 5.5 Can LLMs Follow “Fake” Knowledge Cutoff Prompts?

claim: Even when a constrained prompt does lower accuracy, the result is uninformative: the model could be role-playing a worse forecaster while still holding the memorized outcome.
quote: Yet, even if constrained prompts produced lower accuracy, theory explains why this result would be equally uninformative: forecasting performance is not identified, consistent with the model having memorized the outcome and role-playing as a worse forecaster

claim: Using a small post-cutoff sample as a 'robustness check' against a large pre-cutoff sample is invalid: low power means that comparing pre- and post-cutoff accuracy cannot separate skill from memorization, so post-cutoff data should be the primary analysis.
quote: Consequently, if post-cutoff data are sufficient to be informative, they should be the primary analysis, not a robustness check; if they are insufficient, comparing pre- and post-cutoff accuracy fails to distinguish skill from memorization.
section: 2 Post-Cutoff Data and the Identification Problem (Proposition 2)

claim: Masking fails: from entity-neutered earnings-call transcripts, GPT-4o identified the firm in 100% of Apple, Meta and Microsoft calls and above 85% for every Magnificent Seven firm, and got Apple's quarter and year right 93.2% of the time.
quote: the company in 100% of Apple, Meta, and Microsoft calls and in above 85% of the calls for all Magnificent Seven firms.3 For Apple, the model achieves 93.2% accuracy in identifying the correct quarter and year.

claim: Recommended mitigation: evaluate LLM forecasting only on data after the model's training cutoff, where memorization is impossible.
quote: To ensure methodological integrity, evaluations of LLMs’ forecasting capabilities should focus exclusively on data beyond their training cutoff, where memorization is impossible.

claim: Prompts that simulate an earlier knowledge cutoff 'unlearned' direct facts about 82.5% of the time and semantic shifts about 70.0% of the time, averaged over three LLMs and two prompts. For causally related events the rate was only about 19.2%.
quote: with average unlearning success rates of around 82.5% and 70.0%, respectively. However, it achieves only about 19.2% on the Counterfactual subset, showcasing its limitation on forgetting causally related events.

claim: Prompted knowledge cutoffs work when the post-cutoff fact is asked about directly, but they fail to suppress post-cutoff knowledge that is causally related to the query without being mentioned in it.
quote: These results demonstrate that while prompt-based knowledge cutoffs are effective when the forgotten information is explicitly queried, they struggle to induce forgetting of information that is not directly mentioned but is causally related to the query.

claim: Method: factual and counterfactual items are posed as two-option multiple choice, one option matching the model's real cutoff and one matching the simulated cutoff. 'Unlearning' counts as success when the model switches its answer after the cutoff prompt.
quote: we convert raw examples into multiple-choice questions with two answer options: one corresponding to the model’s original knowledge cutoff, and the other aligned with the simulated cutoff. Unlearning is considered successful if the model changes its response following the cutoff prompt.

claim: Reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o3) did much better than non-reasoning models on the counterfactual subset, which the authors take to mean that counterfactual evaluation depends on causal reasoning rather than recall.
quote: Reasoning models substantially outperform non-reasoning ones on the Counterfactual subset, supporting that counterfactual evaluation critically depends on causal reasoning rather than mere recall.

claim: Counterfactual-subset unlearning success (Table 1, prompts P1/P2): DeepSeek-R1 0.723/0.701, o3 0.478/0.533, DeepSeek-V3 0.152/0.125, GPT-4o 0.144/0.201. Non-reasoning models rarely set aside causally downstream post-cutoff knowledge.

The authors still read the results as partly positive: every model showed some unlearning on every subset, so prompted cutoffs improve fairness in temporal evaluation, though they do not eliminate leakage.
quote: We also observe that all three LLMs exhibit some degree of unlearning across all subsets, indicating that prompted knowledge cutoffs consistently improve fairness in temporal evaluation settings.

claim: Suggested reasons for unlearning failures: some pretraining data lack timestamps, and cutoff-simulation prompts likely never appeared in the models' instruction-tuning data.
quote: one contributing factor may be the lack of timestamps in some of the LLM pretraining data. Another possible reason is that the prompts to simulate knowledge cutoff have not appeared in the instruction finetuning datasets for these LLMs.

claim: Limitation: only prompting was tested, not other unlearning methods. Instruction-tuning models on cutoff prompts is proposed as future work.
quote: One limitation of this study is that we did not explore unlearning methods beyond prompting, primarily due to constraints in data and computational resources.

claim: Across 477 competition forecasting questions and 9 models, Simulated Ignorance (prompting the model to ignore knowledge after a cutoff) does not reproduce True Ignorance: a 52% gap remains, and chain-of-thought does not suppress prior knowledge even when the traces look clean.
quote: we find that SI fails systematically: (1) cutoff instructions leave a 52% performance gap between SI and TI; (2) chain-of-thought reasoning fails to suppress prior knowledge, even when reasoning traces contain no explicit post-cutoff references;

claim: Adding a cutoff instruction closes only 48% of the Brier-score gap between pre-cutoff (SI) and post-cutoff (TI) questions, and every model still shows a significant gap.
quote: Quantitatively, the cutoff closes 48% of the SI–TI gap, leaving 52% unexplained (Fig. 2B). All models still show significant gaps under the cutoff prompt. SI therefore remains an unreliable proxy for TI even with explicit temporal constraints.
section: 4.1 Layer 1: Cutoff Instructions Reduce but Do Not Eliminate the Gap

claim: How much of the gap the cutoff prompt closes depends on domain: 91% for business questions (BUS) but only 33% for politics/geopolitics, which the authors attribute to event salience.
quote: The SI–TI gap varies substantially across domains: cutoff instructions close 91% of the gap in the most responsive domain (BUS) but only 33% in the least responsive (POLGEO).
section: 4.1 Layer 1: Cutoff Instructions Reduce but Do Not Eliminate the Gap

claim: Reasoning-optimized models produce cleaner, more compliant traces but larger SI-TI Brier gaps than non-reasoning models (0.086 vs 0.064 with direct prompting plus cutoff; 0.097 vs 0.067 with CoT plus cutoff).
quote: However, reasoning-optimized models exhibit larger SI– TI gaps than non-reasoning models (Fig. 5B): 0.086 vs. 0.064 under G1′, and 0.097 vs. 0.067 under G2′.
section: 4.3 Layer 3: Reasoning-Optimized Models Show Cleaner Traces but Larger Gaps

claim: Cross-model natural experiment: the same Q4 2024 questions scored Brier 0.136 for DeepSeek-V3.2, for which they are pre-cutoff, and 0.204 for GPT-5.1, for which they are post-cutoff. The gap tracks each model's cutoff, not question difficulty.
quote: The same questions yield Brier 0.136 for DeepSeek but 0.204 for GPT-5.1. The only variable is whether the questions fall before or after each model’s cutoff—strong evidence that the gap reflects leakage, not difficulty.
section: 5.1 Difficulty Control: The Gap Is Model-Specific, Not Calendar-Specific

claim: Difficulty control with human forecasters: Metaculus humans did about equally well on pre- and post-cutoff questions (Brier difference 0.011), while the models' pre/post difference was about 0.13, an order of magnitude larger.
quote: Humans find both splits equally difficult (∆= 0.011), while models show gaps an order of magnitude larger (∆≈ 0.13). This confirms that the model gap reflects leaked knowledge, not question difficulty.

claim: Recommendations: avoid pre-cutoff evaluation by using only questions after every model's cutoff or continuously refreshed benchmarks, and detect leakage with performance gaps rather than reasoning-trace audits.
quote: Avoid pre-cutoff evaluation. Restrict to questions genuinely postdating all models’ cutoffs, or use continuously refreshed benchmarks. 2. Do not trust clean traces. Performance-based metrics (SI–TI gaps) are more reliable than trace audits for detecting leakage.

claim: Limitations: only prompt-based interventions were tested (parameter-level unlearning is left open), and only binary questions were evaluated.
quote: We test only prompt-based interventions; whether parameter-level approaches (e.g., machine unlearning) could achieve better SI fidelity remains open [Liu et al., 2024]. Finally, our evaluation focuses on binary questions; other formats may differ.

claim: Search-engine date filters leak heavily. At least one retrieved page carried major post-cutoff information for 71.0% of questions on Google's before: filter and 81.2% on DuckDuckGo's date-range filter, and a page directly revealed the answer for 41.0% and 54.8% respectively.
quote: at least one document with major leakage (score ≥3) appears for 71.0% of questions on Google and 81.2% on DuckDuckGo, and at least one document directly reveals the answer (score 4) for 41.0% and 54.8%, respectively.

claim: Leaked documents inflate measured forecasting skill: gpt-oss-120b's Brier score fell from 0.24 with leak-free documents to 0.10 with strong-to-direct leakage.
quote: access to leaky content inflates apparent accuracy, reducing the Brier score from 0.24 with leak-free documents to 0.10 with strong-to-direct leakage.

claim: Page metadata is unreliable as an availability proxy: a page reporting a 2020 last-update contained a 2023 fact (Finland joining NATO). This lets leakage slip past pipelines that re-filter on extracted publication or update dates.
quote: a retrieved page reports as last updated in 2020 yet contains text stating Finland joined NATO in 2023 and other facts in 2024, yielding a direct leakage (Score 4). This mechanism can bypass pipelines that double check retrieval by filtering on extracted publication or update dates.

claim: Four recurring leakage mechanisms: in-place page updates, related-content modules such as sidebars, absence-based signals (a comprehensive timeline that omits an event), and unreliable metadata.
quote: We further characterize four recurring leakage mechanisms: page updates, related-content modules, absence-based signals, and unreliable metadata.

claim: Older cutoffs leak more: more than 46% of retrieved URLs held post-cutoff information for 2021-2022 questions, against 34.5%/31.4% (Google/DuckDuckGo) for 2023 and 26.6%/27.7% for 2025.
quote: search results for the earliest questions (2021–2022) exhibit a consistently high density of post-cutoff information across both engines (>46%). The 2023 cohort shows a notable drop (Google 34.5%, DuckDuckGo 31.4%), followed by a further decrease in 2025 (Google 26.6%, DuckDuckGo 27.7%).

claim: Method: about 100 unique URLs per question were retrieved through each engine's date filter, with the cutoff set to the question's opening date on the forecasting platform.
quote: retrieved approximately 100 unique URLs per question via Google Search’s before: filter and DuckDuckGo’s date-range filter (start date 2000-01-01), with the cutoff set to the question’s opening date on the forecasting platform

claim: Recommended mitigation: stronger retrieval safeguards or frozen, time-stamped web snapshots. The failure applies to any pipeline that treats date filters as enough to keep out post-cutoff information.
quote: We recommend stronger retrieval safeguards or evaluation on frozen, time-stamped web snapshots. While our experiments focus on RF, the failure mode is general: pipelines that treat search-engine date filters as sufficient to prevent post-cutoff information from entering the retrieval

claim: Limitation: the paper quantifies the leakage but does not test mitigations such as Wayback Machine retrieval or frozen snapshot databases.
quote: Finally, we diagnose and quantify the leakage problem but do not experimentally evaluate mitigation strategies such as Wayback Machine retrieval or frozen snapshot databases.

claim: The standard contamination check for LLM backtests (comparing scores before and after the training cutoff) is uninformative: four flagship models fail it on questions that all resolved after their cutoffs, so they cannot have memorized the answers.
quote: The standard check for contamination in LLM backtests is simple: compare scores before and after the training cutoff. We show this check is uninformative. Four flagship models fail it on questions they cannot have memorized: every scored question resolved after their cutoffs.

claim: Four of five flagship models were flagged with spurious 'leakage' gaps of +0.044 to +0.061 even though every scored question resolved after their cutoffs. Recency alone produced the pattern.
quote: Result: four of five flagships are flagged, ∆= +0.044 to +0.061∗; recency alone produces the leakage pattern.

claim: The reverse inference fails too: a flat pre/post profile does not show a backtest is clean, because an honest model with the same recency profile scores identically. Passive scores only partially identify the leakage inflation.
quote: The practical consequence corrects common practice: a flat pre/post performance profile is not evidence of a clean backtest, because an honest model with the same recency profile produces identical scores.

claim: Leakage is not a uniform rate. Half the leaked signal already yields three quarters of the full inflation, and leakage concentrates on outcomes that surprised the crowd and that training data covered densely.
quote: half the leaked signal already yields three quarters of the full inflation. Leakage concentrates where the crowd was surprised and training coverage was dense, so an average contamination rate is the wrong audit object.

claim: Recommended audit: pick an external reference, either a known cutoff (regression discontinuity) or a matched clean control model (difference-in-differences), run the matching estimator, and report a leakage-adjusted score with its assumption. Paraphrase probes can only detect leakage.
quote: Choose a reference—a known cutoff (regression discontinuity) or a matched clean control (difference-in-differences)—run the matching estimator, and report the leakage-adjusted score with its assumption; paraphrase probes only detect.

claim: One frontier detection: GPT-5.5 shows a significant boundary jump of +0.078 (CI +0.057 to +0.124) at its documented December 2025 cutoff.
quote: The jump at GPT-5.5’s December 2025 cutoff is +0.078 (CI [+0.057, +0.124], n = 60/339 at ±90 days).
section: 7.3 One detection: a boundary signature for GPT-5.5

claim: Naive pre/post gaps that looked like leakage disappeared after a pre-registered, profile-matched difference-in-differences adjustment. Using a weak, mismatched control (GPT-3.5-Turbo) inflated the estimate to +0.055.
quote: Naive gaps again look like leakage, but after the paired, profile-matched DiD, no adjusted estimate is significantly positive (Figure 4). Substituting GPT-3.5-Turbo raises the primary estimate to +0.055, as a weak control should.
section: 7.2 Disciplined nulls under the matched control

claim: Limitation: the null results only have power against boundary-differential inflation above floors of 0.046-0.098. Uniform inflation across the whole training window would go undetected.
quote: the M5 nulls have power against boundary-differential inflation above their floors (0.046 to 0.098), not against uniform inflation over the training window (Section 7.2).

claim: When popular LLM trading agents are re-run on market data from after their backbone LLM's release, the best-performing agent's returns drop by 50%, which the authors call a 'profit mirage' caused by information leakage.
quote:
The best-performing LLM-based agent also drop 50%! The
dazzling return collapses to a statistical zero once the model is no
longer allowed to peek at the future it was trained on.

claim: Across the published LLM agents tested, Sharpe ratio fell by 51.48%-62.23% and total return by 50.18%-71.85% between the pre-cutoff backtest period and the post-cutoff period.
quote:
The Sharpe
Ratio decay ranges from 51.48% (QuantAgent) to 62.23% (FinCON),
while the Total Return decay ranges from 50.18% (TradingAgents)
to 71.85% (FinMem).

claim: The leakage test compares a pre-cutoff backtest window (Q2-Q3 2021) with a post-cutoff window (Q3-Q4 2024) chosen so the market returns were nearly equal, so market conditions cannot explain the performance drop.
quote:
a historical trade period (Q2-Q3 2021, backtesting setting)
and a latest trade period (Q3-Q4 2024, generalization setting ). No-
tably, the market returns in the two periods are similar (market
return is +13.79% and +13.35%), to minimize the impact of the mar-
ket itself.

claim: To detect leakage, the authors build counterfactual inputs by changing or removing key events such as earnings reports, replacing price series, and altering technical and fundamental factors, then check whether the model's predictions respond.
quote:
Counterfactual market environments[3]
are constructed by perturbing inputs: modifying or removing key
events (e.g., earnings reports, regulatory changes), replacing price

technical indicators

claim: Under counterfactual perturbations, FinMem kept over 82% of its predictions unchanged (prediction consistency 0.8213, confidence invariance 0.8743), meaning it largely ignored the changed inputs and relied on memory.
quote:
FinMem exhibits the highest leakage, with a PC of
0.8213 and CI of 0.8743, indicating over 82% of predictions remain
unchanged despite perturbations, with stable confidence, reflecting
heavy reliance on memorized patterns.

claim: On the FinLeak-Bench memorization audit, frontier LLMs recalled past market facts with high average accuracy, from 85.37% (price inquiries) to 92.94% (event impacts).
quote:
All models exhibit high average accuracy across question types,
ranging from 85.37% for price inquiries to 92.94% for event impacts.

claim: Fine-tuning two open models on financial data raised in-distribution accuracy but cut accuracy on unseen data by 21.53% and 18.06%, which the authors read as overfitting to leaked data.
quote:
Critically, generalization ca-
pability declines substantially, with reductions of 21.53% and 18.06%
in accuracy on unseen data, confirming that fine-tuning leads to
overfitting on leaked data.

claim: The proposed mitigation (FactFin) uses the LLM to generate strategies rather than make trading decisions directly, and adds a counterfactual simulator. The authors report it had the lowest leakage metrics on every test asset.
quote:
Our FactFin, through Monte Carlo Tree Search
and a Counterfactual Simulator, uses the LLM as a strategy genera-
tor rather than a direct decision-maker, substantially reducing PC
and CI while increasing IDS, achieving the lowest leakage across
all assets.

Of the 75 papers with a trading test, 51% deduct no trading costs and only 9%

months or shorter.

Before coding a single paper we pre-registered a population of 91 papers from a

claim: The authors propose a minimum reporting standard for LLM trading results. It includes the dated test window and number of assets, the model's training cutoff and whether the test is after it, a cost model with breakeven cost, and the number of strategies, prompts or configurations searched.

claim: Stated limitations: LLMs did the coding, the verbatim-quote check only shows that a code points to real text and not that the judgement is right, and the blind second pass covered just 18 papers.
quote:
The coders were language models. The quote check guarantees
that each code points to real text, not that the judgement is right; the second pass bounds
disagreement at about one paper in ten on the subjective fields, on 18 papers only.

claim: On a look-ahead-free event benchmark covering pre-earnings and post-bad-news trades, no LLM agent from any vendor beat simple bets. Before earnings, the agents mostly just bought and earned what an always-buy rule earned.
quote:
Across five models from four vendors, no agent
beat the simple bets. Before earnings, the agents mostly bought
and earned what buying before every announcement earned

quote:
The only gains came from what the models had memorized in
training. Given only the ticker and the dates, a GPT-based model
called the direction of 59.2% of the announcements before its
training cutoff and 53.3% after it.

claim: Splitting at the training cutoff exposed the memorized gain. On pre-cutoff announcements one agent's named run beat its blind run by +30.3 bp per announcement. After the cutoff the gap reversed to −22.0 bp and the named run lost −25.5 bp.
quote:
the named run beat the blind run by +30.3 bp on those
announcements (95% interval +16.5 to +46.2). After the cutoff
the gap turned negative, −22.0 bp (−44.9 to +0.2), and the
named run earned −25.5 bp per announcement

quote:
An audit found
0 inputs published after the decision close, and a scan
of 4,830 blind prompts found 0 leaked tickers, names or
dates

In our runs, splitting the decision into
steps rarely changed what an agent earned, peers, short selling
and insider filings moved the alpha by a few basis points, and a

into passes until we raised it

Run Blind, Split at the Cutoff and Probe Memory. A profit
from a named run on old events should not be reported until
the same agent shows it blind and on events after its training

quote:
The blind prompts mask tickers, names
and dates, but a model may still recognize a famous quarter
or crash from the market moves around it.

run, and we do not rank models. The clean tests hold 75
announcements and 53 drops, enough to show a direction but

quote:
Our results demonstrate that standard LLMs exhibit signif-
icant lookahead bias, with alpha decay exceeding -15 per-
centage points between periods, while Pitinf models main-
tain stable performance.

Our evaluation compares model performance across two
carefully selected periods to test models with knowledge
cutoffs through 2023-2024, while maintaining similar mar-
ket characteristics for fair comparison, like in FinLeak-

claim: Standard models lost alpha between periods: Llama 3.1 8B by -17.23 pp, Llama 3.1 70B by -15.25 pp, and DeepSeek 3.2 by -21.77 pp (columns: P1 return, P1 alpha, P2 return, P2 alpha, alpha decay).

perior memorization of 2021 data, it suffered the most

agent configurations on all tasks, with result

Among the 193 result-pass records with PIT
violations, targeted single-event perturbations ex-
posed non-rounding discrepancies in 111 and ex-
ecution failures in two more (113/193, 58.5%).

Temporal-semantic misuse.

ing business-valid time, information availability,

of submissions, respectively.

We have not
isolated PIT violations’ contribution to result fail-
ure. Look-ahead bias from model pretraining is

claim: The LLM judge's overall scores for the two systems were nearly identical (7.44 vs 7.40, p=0.584), while HindSight mean scores were 0.297 vs 0.119 (p<0.001).

claim: A zero outcome score is not proof an idea is bad: it may not have been pursued within the 30-month window, or its matching papers may lie outside the 10-topic pool.
