claim: For one of the four models the harness had no detectable effect, and the formal model x harness interaction test was not significant at 5%, so the model-specificity is a pattern in their data, not an established effect.
quote: For one of the four models the harness has no detectable effect at all. The formal test of the model × harness interaction fell short of the 5% level, so the model-specificity is a consistent pattern in our data rather than an established effect.

claim: The same model (qwen3.8-flash-next) was the most compliant under the reviewer harness (93.6%) and the least compliant when the policy was reachable only through search (82.1%).
quote: qwen3.8-flash-next is the most compliant model under the reviewer harness (93.6%) and the least compliant when the policy is reachable only through search (82.1%)
section: Results: The harness effect depends on the model

claim: For 2 of four models, swapping the harness moved compliance by more than any between-model difference under a fixed harness (at most 7.7 points), and the model ranking changed with the harness.
quote: For 2 of our four models, swapping the harness moved compliance by more than any difference between models under a fixed harness (at most 7.7 points), and the ranking of models changed with the harness.

claim: Adding a same-model compliance reviewer removed 33% of violations without increasing over-refusals, contrary to the authors' pre-registered prediction.
quote: A same-model reviewer helps and, here, costs nothing. It removes 33% of violations and does not increase over-refusals, against both our prediction and recent evidence of high false rejection by same-model reviewers (Tanveer, 2026).

claim: For rules that are arithmetic (date windows, cumulative limits), which failed under every harness, the authors argue the right control is deterministic code in the harness rather than another model call.
quote: Where a rule is arithmetic (a date window, a cumulative limit), the natural control is deterministic code in the harness (Yu et al., 2026b), not another model call.

claim: 26% of violations were invisible in the conversation because the agent denied what it had done. The authors therefore recommend evaluating the model-harness pair, reporting the harness, and scoring executed actions rather than transcripts.
quote: 26% of violations were invisible in the conversation because the agent denied what it had done. Banks, supervisors and benchmark authors should evaluate the model–harness pair, report the harness, and score executed actions.

claim: Limitation: only moderate-size open-weight models with reasoning disabled were tested, and stronger or reasoning models may change the harness effects. 7 of 11 rule families were near ceiling, which limited power.
quote: moderate size on one domestic API, with reasoning disabled; stronger or reasoning models may close the date arithmetic gap and change the harness effects. 7 of 11 rule families were near ceiling outside H2, which limits power for the harness comparisons

claim: This position paper argues that, among models of comparable frontier capability on long-horizon tasks, the execution harness (context, tools, orchestration, verification) often determines agent performance more than the model does.
quote: the agent execution harness, namely the infrastructure layer that governs context construction, tool interaction, orchestration, and verification around a language model, is often a stronger determinant of agent performance than the model it wraps.

claim: A harness tuned around one model can score lower with another model. The authors' controlled grid showed six ranking reversals across nine model-pair/harness-pair comparisons.
quote: The LangChain Terminal-Bench result shows the same coupling, where a harness tuned around one model yields a lower score when paired with another [36]. Our controlled grid confirms this under matched conditions: six ranking reversals across nine model-pair / harness-pair comparisons.

claim: On SWE-bench Pro, six frontier models spanned only 4.9 points under one standardized scaffold, while holding Claude Opus 4.5 fixed and changing only the harness produced a 9.5-point spread.
quote: six leading frontier models span only 4.9 percentage points under the standardized SEAL scaffold (41.0% to 45.9%). Holding Claude Opus 4.5 fixed and varying only the harness widens this to 9.5 points (SEAL vs Claude Code).

claim: In the controlled model-by-harness grid, average harness-induced variance (18.48) was 7.80× the model-induced variance (2.37). Changing the harness moved a fixed model by 8.5 to 13.0 points, while changing the model under a fixed harness moved scores by 2.5 to 5.0 points.
quote: Average HV is 18.48 pp2 versus average MV of 2.37 pp2, a ratio of 7.80×. Changing the harness moves GLM5.1 by 13.0 percentage points and GPT-5.4 and Kimi K2.6 by 8.5 points each. Changing the model within a fixed harness moves scores by only 3.0, 2.5, and 5.0 points for H1, H2, H3.

claim: The authors explicitly do not claim the 7.80× harness/model variance ratio is universal, only that harness variance can dominate under controlled conditions.
quote: We do not claim that the 7.80× ratio is universal. The grid demonstrates that harness variance can dominate model variance under controlled conditions and that the decomposition protocol produces interpretable estimates on a realistic task distribution.

claim: The controlled evidence is small and coding-only: a 100-task SWE-bench Verified subset with two runs per cell under a fixed environment, 50-step budget and 120-second per-step timeout.
quote: on a difficulty-stratified 100-task subset of SWE-bench Verified [13]. Each (Mi, Hj) cell uses two independent runs with shared task order, Docker execution environment, SWE-bench evaluation pipeline, 50-step budget, and 120-second per-step timeout.

claim: The paper prescribes that the harness behind a score be part of the reported experimental condition, and that cross-model comparisons either lock the harness or vary it as a controlled factor.
quote: The harness used to produce a benchmark score must be part of the experimental condition, and cross-model comparisons must hold the harness fixed (locked-harness protocol) or vary it as a controlled factor (factorial protocol).

claim: Limitation: the public leaderboard evidence is observational. Harnesses differ on many dimensions and engineering budgets, so it cannot isolate which components drive the variance.
quote: But public evidence is observational. Public harnesses differ across many dimensions and were built by different teams with different engineering budgets, so the public data do not isolate which harness components drive the variance.

claim: Model rankings reversed across harnesses: on Terminal-Bench 4 Claude led GPT by 7.94 points in OpenHands but trailed it by 30.16 points in PI.
quote: Model rankings reverse across harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 4, Claude leads GPT by 7.94 points in OpenHands but trails it by 30.16 points in PI.

claim: For four of five models the best harness changed from one benchmark to another, though some pairings held (openJiuwen was Kimi's best on all three benchmarks, by 5.61 to 11.11 points).
quote: For four of the five models, the best harness changes from one benchmark to another, yet some pairings hold: openJiuwen gives Kimi its highest score on all three benchmarks, by 5.61 to 11.11 points.

claim: A model's own vendor harness was not reliably its best, and higher cost did not reliably buy a higher score; GPT scored higher under a lean harness at less than a quarter of the cost per task.
quote: A model’s own vendor harness is not reliably its best, and higher cost does not reliably buy a higher score. On Terminal-Bench 4, GPT scores higher under PI than under DSH at less than a quarter of the cost per task.

claim: The trajectories suggest fit depends on whether the harness returns failures in a form the model can use: GPT did best with a lean scaffold, while Kimi, which often issues malformed tool calls, did best in a harness that catches them.
quote: Models start almost all repairs themselves, so much depends on whether the harness hands failures back in a form the model can use. GPT does best with PI’s lean scaffold, while Kimi, which often issues malformed tool calls, does best in openJiuwen.

claim: In failed runs the final self-check rested on evidence the agent produced itself. 35 self-certified reports that were nonetheless graded as failures show that self-checking cannot replace an external acceptance criterion.
quote: the evidence a final check rests on is therefore produced by the agent itself. The 35 self-certified reports show that checking cannot substitute for supplying the criterion against which to check.

claim: Limitation: one counted run per task, with model settings, tools and budgets not uniformly matched, so no single component's causal effect is isolated and run-to-run variance is unmeasured.
quote: on three fixed task subsets with one counted run per task. Model settings, tools, and execution budgets are not uniformly matched, so the observed differences do not isolate the causal effect of any single component, and run-to-run variance is not measured.

claim: Across 66 configurations, model rankings, each model's best harness, and the standing of native pairings all depended on the task setting.
quote: Across 66 configurations, model rankings, the best harness for each model, and the standing of native pairings all depend on the task setting, while some pairings, such as openJiuwen with Kimi, stay ahead on all three benchmarks.

claim: The paper cites contrasting prior evidence: the ALE-Claw analysis found more spread across models than across harnesses, and a lean harness that kept accuracy at lower cost.
quote: The ALE-Claw analysis finds a larger spread across models than across harnesses and, in its tested settings, a lean harness that retains accuracy at lower cost [7].

claim: On investment-management tasks, curated domain skills (procedure docs plus executable components) raised mean scores from 0.366 to 0.528, with the largest gains in portfolio construction and risk management. Self-generated skills gave little benefit at higher cost.
quote: curated skills consistently improve performance, raising mean scores from 0.366 to 0.528, with the largest gains in portfolio construction and risk management. In contrast, self-generated skills provide little benefit despite higher computational cost.

claim: Point-in-time discipline is enforced through an explicit as_of_date per episode, system prompts forbidding post-date information, and tools that return only point-in-time slices.
quote: First, all episodes carry an explicit as_of_date; system prompts forbid reliance on post-date information and tooling returns only point-in-time slices.

claim: Domain gains were uneven: curated skills added +0.278 in portfolio construction and +0.218 in risk management, but only +0.054 in fundamental analysis (0.458 to 0.512).
Skill gains varied by model and were not larger for stronger models: gpt-4.1 gained +0.405, gpt-5.4 only +0.091, and claude-sonnet-4.6, from the strongest no-skill baseline (0.534), gained +0.125.
quote: Curated skills do not simply help stronger models more. The largest gain accrues to gpt-4.1 (+0.405), while gpt-5.4 sees a smaller +0.091 gain and claude-sonnet-4.6 starts from the strongest no-skill baseline (0.534) and gains +0.125.

claim: The same skills-plus-tools treatment gave a +32.5 pp uplift under the Hermes harness, almost double the +16.2 pp under the FinSkillBench harness, so the measured gain depends on the harness.
quote: the +32.5 pp aggregate Hermes uplift measures the same combined effect of skill documents and executable tool access. This is almost two times higher than the +16.2 pp curated skills uplift from the FinSkillBench agent harness.

claim: A single benchmark with a single harness can under- or overestimate skill effects depending on where its baselines sit, so the authors recommend reporting effects stratified by baseline level.
quote: A single benchmark and a single harness can therefore underestimate or overestimate skill effects depending on where its baselines sit. We recommend that future benchmarks report skill effects stratified by baseline level, not only as a single aggregate number.

claim: Evaluation design choices change conclusions: dropping invalid or max-turn submissions inflates scores, and letting no-skill agents call the same deterministic solvers confounds the measured skill effect.
quote: if invalid and max-turn submissions are dropped, score estimates are inflated relative to deploymentlike reliability; if no-skill agents can call the same deterministic solvers as curated agents, the measured skill effect is confounded

claim: Limitation: agent-loop variance is unmeasured (one sample per cell), especially in the 21% of calls that exhausted the turn budget.
quote: We acknowledge this leaves agent-loop variance unmeasured, particularly in turn-budget-exhausted episodes (21% of calls), and flag it as a target for future expansion.

claim: On Portuguese financial commentaries, item-level agreement between LLM judges and human annotators averaged 27.2%, below the 42.1% agreement seen within the LLM group and within the human group, so LLM judges were not more internally consistent than humans.
quote: Cross-group agreement averages 27.2%, below the within-group agreement observed among both LLMs and humans (42.1% in each group). This indicates that LLM judges are not more internally consistent than human experts.

claim: The two human annotators (a linguist and a financial expert) agreed on only 42.1% of items (Cohen's kappa 0.30, vs 17.5% chance), which the authors read as different evaluation stances rather than noise.
quote: The linguist (L) and the financial expert (F) agreed on 42.1% of items (Cohen’s κ = 0.30), a level of agreement that, while modest, sits well above the 17.5% expected by chance and reflects distinct evaluation stances rather than annotation noise.

claim: The best pairwise human-LLM agreement was only 36.8% (Claude vs linguist and Gemini vs financial expert), and agreement rates and ranking similarity gave different pictures of alignment.
quote: the highest human–LLM agreement is 36.8%, observed for both Claude–linguist and Gemini–financial expert. However, Gemini and the linguist show the closest Elo-based rankings (Table 1), suggesting that agreement rates and ranking similarity capture complementary aspects of alignment.

claim: Command-R+ got no votes from any LLM judge yet was the financial expert's top model (24.6% of their preferences); the expert's reasons stressed structured financial reasoning and actionable insight.
quote: Its generations receive no votes from LLM judges, yet F ranks the model first overall, with Command-R+ accounting for 24.6% of F’s preferences. F’s justifications emphasize structured financial reasoning and actionable insight

claim: In the order-sensitive sequential knockout protocol, the starting commentary won 28.1% of rounds against a 25% random baseline, so initial position had at most a minor effect.
quote: The starting commentary wins in 28.1% of the rounds, only slightly above the random expectation of 25% for four candidates per round, suggesting that the initial position has at most a minor influence on the outcome.

claim: The commentaries LLM judges picked as winners tended to have lower CTC factuality-metric scores than the alternatives (Qwen3 73.7%, Opus 63.6%, Gemini 57.9% of comparisons).
quote: Final winners have lower CTC scores than their al- ternatives in 57.1% of comparisons overall, with this effect concentrated among LLM judges (Qwen3: 73.7%, Opus: 63.6%, Gemini: 57.9%).

claim: The study used only 19 material facts, a sample the authors say may limit statistical precision.
quote: Our analysis is based on 19 material facts, reflecting both the feasibility of annotation [Sandan et al. 2025] and our focus on the highest-scoring candidate set. This limited sample size may affect statistical precision.

claim: Under identical guidelines (criterion selection optional), LLM judges almost always named a criterion and humans often did not, so the two kinds of output are hard to compare even with the same rubric.
quote: LLMs tend to point to at least one criterion, whereas humans do not. This is another point to consider when comparing LLM and human evaluation: even when using the same evaluation guidelines, they may produce different outputs that are difficult to compare.

claim: The study built 200 generated stock-move articles with causal-mechanism explanations from Chinese market data and compared three frontier LLM judges against human annotations, zero-shot and few-shot.
quote: We construct 200 articles from Chinese stock market data and compare Gemini 3.5 Flash, GPT-5.5, and Claude Opus 5 with human annotations under zero-shot and few-shot settings.

claim: LLM-human agreement on causal-explanation Completeness (Pearson r 0.679-0.775) was consistently higher than on Relevance (r 0.557-0.664).
quote: Completeness consistently showed higher agreement than Relevance. Across both prompting settings, Pearson’s r ranged from 0.557 to 0.664 for Relevance, compared with 0.679 to 0.775 for Completeness.

claim: On the categorical Economic Plausibility dimension, zero-shot agreement with the human varied widely by judge: kappa 0.591 (GPT-5.5), 0.522 (Gemini 3.5 Flash) and 0.326 (Claude Opus 5).
quote: For Economic Plausibility, GPT-5.5 achieved the highest agreement under zero-shot prompting (κ = 0.591), followed by Gemini 3.5 Flash (κ = 0.522) and Claude Opus 5 (κ = 0.326).

claim: LLM judges scored more harshly than the human annotator: human means were 4.145 (Relevance) and 3.770 (Completeness), while LLM means ranged 3.265-4.125 and 3.005-3.915.
quote: The human mean scores were 4.145 for Relevance and 3.770 for Completeness, while the LLM means ranged from 3.265 to 4.125 and from 3.005 to 3.915, respectively. This indicates that LLM judges generally adopted a more conservative scoring standard

claim: A matched-subset test that controls for quality with judge-minus-human F-score residuals found no statistically significant self-preference bias for Gemini or GPT.
quote: Within our experimental setup and matched dataset, neither Gemini nor GPT showed statistically significant self-preference bias in the F-score residual, Pearson correlation, or EP agreement analyses.

claim: Few-shot prompting significantly lowered agreement with the human on Economic Plausibility for all three judges (kappa change -0.067 to -0.240), so demonstrations did not reliably help.
quote: For Economic Plausibility, agreement significantly decreased for all three judges. The changes in κ were −0.067 (95% CI [−0.134, −0.003]) for Claude Opus 5, −0.190 (95% CI [−0.318, −0.061]) for GPT-5.5, and −0.240 (95% CI [−0.368, −0.100]) for Gemini 3.5 Flash.

claim: The human reference came from a single annotator, which the authors say limits its reliability and rules out measuring inter-annotator agreement.
quote: relying on a single annotator limits the reliability of the human evaluation and prevents direct assessment of inter-annotator agreement.

claim: The authors present their results only as preliminary evidence that an LLM judge can work for reference-free evaluation of causal-mechanism explanations, and note that judge behaviour shifts with the evaluation dimension and the prompting strategy.
quote: These results provide preliminary evidence that LLM-as-a-Judge can be useful for reference-free evaluation of causal mechanism explanations in financial news, while also indicating that its evaluation behavior can vary depending on the evaluation dimension and prompting strategy.

claim: The Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test) justifies replacing human annotators with an LLM by comparing the LLM against at least three human annotators on 50-100 examples.
quote: This procedure is simple and requires minimal effort to apply; it involves comparing the LLM to a small group of human annotators (at least three) on a modest subset of examples (between 50 and 100).

claim: Beyond a 30-instance minimum for the t-test, with cost-benefit epsilon = 0.2 the best LLM usually starts passing the test before 100 annotated instances, and in half the datasets before 50.
quote: beyond the minimum requirement of 30 instances to satisfy the normality assumption of the t-test, Figure 2 shows that for ε = 0.2, in most cases, the LLM begins to pass the test before annotating 100 instances, and in half even before 50 instances.

claim: With a stricter epsilon = 0.1, roughly double the instances are needed (100-150), and on three datasets the LLM never passes regardless of sample size.
quote: With ε = 0.1 the alt-test requires more instances, typically double the amount needed for ε = 0.2, between 100 and 150. Yet, in three datasets (LGBTeen, MTBench, and SummEval), the LLM fails to pass the test regardless of the number of instances.

claim: Decision rule: run one t-test per human annotator, correct with Benjamini-Yekutieli FDR, and justify LLM annotations if the winning rate (share of rejected nulls) is at least 0.5.
quote: We then apply the BY procedure to these p-values, which identifies the set of rejected null hypotheses. Finally, we compute the winning rate (the proportion of rejected hypotheses) and if ω ≥0.5, we can statistically justify using LLM annotations.

claim: Rule of thumb for the cost-benefit margin epsilon: 0.2 when the comparison annotators are trusted experts, 0.15 for skilled annotators, and 0.1 for crowd workers.
quote: As a rule of thumb, we recommend setting ε to 0.2 when the annotators are trusted experts and 0.15 when they are skilled annotators (e.g., undergraduate students or trained workers). If the annotators are crowd workers, ε should be set to 0.1.

claim: Across ten datasets, passing depended on the dataset and annotation aspect and LLMs often failed, so LLM annotations cannot be used without this kind of justification.
quote: Our results demonstrate that test success depends on the dataset and annotation aspect, with LLMs often failing to pass it. This emphasizes the relevance of the alt-test: researchers cannot simply rely on LLM annotations without justifying this choice.

claim: For settings with only one expert available, a variant treats that single expert's labels as gold and tests whether the LLM aligns with the expert more closely than non-expert annotators do.
quote: Our modification compares the LLM against non-experts to determine whether the LLM aligns more closely with the single expert than a non-expert does.

claim: Stated limitation: in the single-expert variant, weak or unqualified non-expert comparators can make the LLM look better, and the procedure cannot fully prevent this misuse.
quote: If the non-experts are particularly weak (e.g., inconsistent or unqualified), the LLM may appear to outperform them, and our procedure cannot fully prevent such misuse.

claim: Main theorem: when the judge is no more accurate than the model being evaluated, no debiasing method can cut the required ground-truth labels by more than half.
quote: Our main result shows that when the judge is no more accurate than the evaluated model, no debiasing method can decrease the required amount of ground truth labels by more than half.

claim: Corollary 7: when evaluating state-of-the-art models, LLM judges give at best a factor-two gain in sample efficiency, unless judging is substantially easier than the task itself.
quote: Corollary 7 implies that when evaluating state-of-the-art models, the best we can expect from using LLM judges is a factor-two improvement in sample efficiency. This is unless the judge’s task is substantially easier than the evaluated model’s task.
section: 3.5 Limited gains for evaluating state-of-the-art models

claim: Because frontier models often differ by only a few percentage points, guaranteeing correct rankings without further assumptions would need judge-ground-truth agreement above 99% for every evaluated model.
quote: As it is common for state-of-the-art models to differ in performance by only low single digit percentages, without further assumptions an agreement rate above 99% (for each evaluated model!) would be required to ensure (asymptotically) correct rankings.
section: 2.2 High agreement rate is insufficient for evaluation

claim: Model rankings were strongly perturbed even though the judges looked accurate: 79% (Llama-3 70B) and 84% (GPT-4) accuracy on MMLU, and 85% expert agreement on MT-Bench.
quote: Lama-3 70B has 79% accuracy on MMLU, while GPT-4 has 84%, and the models used in MT-Bench have 85% agreement with expert annotators. Our next proposition explains how it is possible for model rankings to be strongly perturbed despite accurate judges.
section: 2.2 High agreement rate is insufficient for evaluation

claim: On MMLU and MT-Bench, savings of more than a factor two were rare and appeared only when state-of-the-art models judged substantially weaker models.
quote: In experiments on MMLU and MT-Bench, we empirically confirm that sample size savings of more than a factor two are rare: We only observe them when current state-of-the-art models are used to judge substantially weaker models.

claim: Prior applications of prediction-powered inference (PPI) to LLM evaluation rarely raised effective sample size by more than 50%, and never by 100% or more.
quote: These works consistently show that PPI improves efficiency in terms of ground truth labels, but gains in effective sample size rarely exceed 50% and are always below 100%.

claim: At the frontier, LLM judges do not change the order of magnitude of ground-truth labels needed: at best the effective sample size doubles.
quote: Our results show that for evaluating frontier models, LLM judges might fall short of the promise of largely replacing expert labelers: While doubling the effective sample size can be useful for practitioners, the order of magnitude of required ground truth labels remains the same with and without access to LLM judges.

claim: The bound can be escaped: gains above a factor two are possible when evaluating is much easier than doing the task, or when plenty of data exists to train a specialized evaluator.
quote: Thus, for tasks in which evaluation is substantially easier than the task itself, or tasks for which data to train a specialized evaluator is abundant, gains in sample efficiency of more than a factor two are possible even when evaluating models at the frontier.

claim: The availability audit falsified the original data premise: a gapless five-minute grid across trade, mark, index and open interest lasted at most 304.5729166666667 days, so the authors disclosed a revised core-stream definition.
quote: An initial gapless five-minute requirement for trade, mark, index, and open interest failed: the longest unrepaired intersection was 304.5729166666667 days. A disclosed revision made trade, mark, index, and realized funding the core streams

claim: The point-in-time rule: a decision at time t may read only records with availability_time <= t. Funding had no publication timestamp, so event time plus five minutes was assumed and tested with 0/5/10/15-minute sensitivity.
quote: The archive lacks a distinct publication-time field, so the primary analysis uses event time plus five minutes as a research assumption, with 0/5/10/15-minute admission sensitivity. A decision at time t may read only records with availability_time <= t.

claim: On 80 frozen known-rule templates, the deterministic leakage auditor caught 40/40 violations and falsely rejected 0/40 legal templates, but the Wilson intervals make this template-level evidence only.
quote: On 80 frozen known-rule templates, the auditor detected 40/40 violations and rejected 0/40 legal templates; Wilson 95% intervals were 91.24%–100% and 0%–8.76%, so this is template-level evidence.

claim: In null-signal controls, full auditing cut mean false passes from 0.2910 (no audit) to 0.0625 and improved all 10 paths (paired difference -0.2285).
quote: At 5% missingness with availability masking, mean false passes were 0.2910 without auditing, 0.2479 with the basic audit, and 0.0625 with the full audit. Full versus no audit improved all 10 paths; the paired difference was -0.2285 with a path-bootstrap 95% interval [-0.2595, -0.2012]

claim: With a shared DSL and matched valid-candidate budgets, the adaptive audited agent and random search each produced 39 validation-qualified candidates, against 29 for tree GP.
quote: Under a shared DSL and matched valid-candidate budgets, a deterministic adaptive audited agent and random search each produced 39 validation-qualified candidates; tree GP produced 29.

claim: Because the agent only tied random search, the authors rejected search-superiority claims; the agent's lower raw-attempt count did not count as evidence because time-to-first-discovery and resource-normalized runtime were not preregistered outcomes.
quote: The audited agent tied random search on qualified candidates and therefore did not beat both baselines. Raw attempts were lower for the agent, but evaluations to first qualified factor and resource-normalized runtime were not frozen outcomes.

claim: In the one-time holdout, all 23 evaluated runs had positive IC but negative net Sharpe, and none of 460 fee-slippage cells had positive Sharpe: predictive signal did not become economic value.
quote: In the one-time historical holdout, all 23 evaluated runs had positive IC but negative net Sharpe under primary costs, and none of 460 fee–slippage cells had positive Sharpe.

claim: The protocol was hash-locked only after the historical interval had ended, so the authors call the final split a one-time historical holdout rather than a prospective test.
quote: Because the protocol was hash-locked after the historical interval had ended, the last partition is called a one-time historical holdout, not a prospective test.

claim: ForecastBench avoids data leakage by containing only questions about future events whose answers are unknown when forecasts are submitted; questions are automatically generated and the set is regularly updated.
quote: To avoid any possibility of data leakage, ForecastBench is comprised solely of questions about future events that have no known answer at the time of submission.

claim: The authors argue that static (retrospective) forecasting benchmarks are vulnerable because model knowledge cut-offs are only estimated and post-training can inject post-cutoff knowledge, contaminating test sets.
quote: Second, knowledge cut-offs are usually estimated using the time range of pre-training data. Such estimates may not be accurate, and post-training may inject further post-cutoff knowledge into the model, contaminating the test sets.

claim: On the 200-question human subset, superforecasters (Brier 0.096) significantly beat both the general public (0.121) and the best LLM, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (0.122); the best LLM was roughly at the level of the public median.
quote: superforecasters achieve an overall mean Brier score of 0.096, significantly outperforming both the general public (Brier = 0.121, p < 0.001) and the top LLM performer on the 200-item subset (Claude 3.5 Sonnet: Brier = 0.122, p < 0.001)

claim: The best LLM configuration that was not given the human crowd forecast on market questions scored Brier 0.136, worse than LLMs that were given the crowd forecast (the top LLMs on the leaderboard all had it).
quote: The top-performing model without access to the crowd forecast on market questions was less accurate than models with access to the human forecast with a Brier score of 0.136.

claim: Top LLM configurations mostly used a scratchpad prompt plus human crowd forecasts as inputs, while adding retrieved recent news did not improve forecasting performance.
quote: most of the top-performing models use the scratchpad prompt (Figure 5) and use as inputs the human crowd forecasts for market questions. Access to recent topical news related to the questions did not improve performance.

claim: The general-public baseline recruited 500 human forecasters via Prolific and Facebook advertisements.
quote: We recruited 500 human forecasters via Prolific and advertisements on Facebook to participate as representatives of the general public.

claim: The expert baseline recruited 39 superforecasters with strong track records on geopolitical questions for a 9-day forecasting experiment (individual stage, then a group stage).
quote: We recruited 39 superforecasters, who have a strong track record of accurate performance on a diverse set of geopolitical questions, to participate in a 9-day forecasting experiment

claim: Before a market question resolves, forecasts are scored against the platform's previous-day crowd forecast as a proxy for ground truth, so interim scores partly measure agreement with the crowd rather than realized outcomes.
quote: Until then, we evaluate performance by calculating the squared distance between the forecasted value and the platform’s crowd forecast (an aggregate of human forecasts reported on the platform) from the preceding day.

claim: Bench to the Future (BTF) is a 'pastcasting' benchmark: questions whose resolutions are already known, each paired with a large frozen offline corpus of tens of thousands of web pages so LLMs can 'forecast' past events realistically.
quote: a "pastcasting" benchmark with hundreds of high-quality questions for which the resolution is already known. Each question is accompanied by a large offline corpus of tens of thousands of relevant web pages, enabling a way to elicit realistic "forecasts" on past events

claim: The authors note that prospective benchmarks (Metaculus AI benchmark, ForecastBench) eliminate contamination risk but impose long waits between forecast and resolution and make repeated experiments impossible, which motivates pastcasting.
quote: All forecasts in these two benchmarks are prospective. This eliminates the risk of data contamination, but also results in long waiting times between forecast and resolution and makes it impossible to run repeated experiments.

claim: Prior pastcasting work that relied on Google's date-indexing filter to exclude post-cutoff evidence likely suffered data contamination, because that filter is known to be faulty.
quote: The authors likely relied on Google’s date indexing functionality to make sure no evidence after the cutoff date is returned, which is known to be faulty, resulting in issues with data contamination.

claim: BTF has 299 binary questions (87 originally binary, 135 split from multiple-choice, 77 from numeric), but after down-weighting questions correlated by construction the effective sample size is only 178.8.
quote: BTF comprises a set of 299 binary questions, 87 of them from original binary questions, 135 from multiple-choice questions, and 77 from numeric questions (see Table 1). The effective number of questions (manually down-weighting questions that are correlated by construction) is 178.8.

claim: In a live-vs-retro comparison (run on a separate set of questions), pastcasting forecasts were broadly consistent with live forecasting, but the authors say further validation with a larger sample is warranted.
quote: The results indicated that our pastcasting methodology produces forecasts that are broadly consistent with live forecasting, though further validation with a larger sample size is warranted.

claim: Repeated LLM forecasts on the same question sometimes ranged from under 20% on one run to over 80% on another, leading the authors to conclude that single LLM forecasts should not be considered reliable.
quote: sometimes giving probabilities < 20% on one run and > 80% on another. This suggests that single forecasts from an LLM should not be considered reliable.

claim: A stated limitation is possible information leakage because RetroSearch uses live Google searches to fetch pages from the frozen database (even though only previously scraped pages are returned).
quote: One concern with the current implementation of RetroSearch is the potential of information leaking due to our reliance on live Google searches to fetch websites from our RetroSearch database (returning, of course, only previously scraped web pages).

claim: The authors flag an uncontrolled confound (newer models carry more up-to-date crystallized knowledge) and therefore cannot attribute newer models' better pastcasting accuracy entirely to planning, tool use, reasoning, and judgment.
quote: Since this is a confounding variable we don’t control for, we cannot confidently state that newer LLM outperforming older LLMs is entirely due to planning, tool-use, reasoning, and judgment.

claim: Under blind expert review, LLM-generated research ideas were judged more novel than human expert ideas (p < 0.05) but slightly weaker on feasibility.
quote: we find LLM-generated ideas are judged as more novel (p < 0.05) than human expert ideas while being judged slightly weaker on feasibility.

claim: The human study used 49 experts writing ideas and 79 expert reviewers (24 of the reviewers also wrote ideas but never reviewed their own).
quote: In the end, we recruited N =49 experts for writing ideas, and N =79 experts for reviewing ideas. Note that 24 out of the 79 reviewers also participated in the idea writing, and we made sure no reviewer would review their own idea.

claim: Across nearly 300 blind reviews, the AI-ideas-more-novel result (p<0.05) held under multiple-hypothesis correction and across different statistical tests.
quote: Through nearly 300 reviews across all our conditions, we find that AI-generated ideas are judged as more novel than human expert ideas (p<0.05), which holds robustly under multiple hypothesis correction and across different statistical tests.

claim: Treating each idea (its averaged reviews) as one datapoint, mean novelty was 5.62 for AI ideas and 5.78 for AI ideas reranked by a human, versus 4.86 for human expert ideas.
quote: both AI Ideas (µ = 5.62 ± σ = 1.39) and AI Ideas + Human Rerank (µ=5.78±σ=1.07) have higher novelty scores than Human Ideas (µ=4.86±σ=1.26).

claim: The novelty gains may correlate with excitement and overall score and may cost some feasibility, but the study lacked statistical power to conclusively establish these secondary effects.
quote: We find some signs that these gains are correlated with excitement and overall score, and may come at the slight expense of feasibility, but our study size did not have sufficient power to conclusively identify these effects

claim: Expert human reviewers agreed with each other only 56.1% of the time (balanced accuracy on a held-out ranking split) despite detailed rubrics, below the 66.0% found in the NeurIPS 2021 reviewer consistency experiment.
quote: reviewers have a relatively low agreement (56.1%) despite the fact that we have provided detailed explanations for each metric in our review form. As a baseline comparison, the NeurIPS 2021 reviewer consistency experiment found 66.0% accuracy

claim: Every LLM evaluator tested (direct scoring, pairwise ranking, 'AI Scientist' reviewer) agreed with expert rankings less than experts agree with each other; the best, a Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker, reached only 53.3% vs. 56.1% human inter-reviewer consistency.
quote: All of these LLM evaluators have a lower agreement than our expert reviewers’ scores. Even the best LLM evaluator — our own Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker — only achieves an accuracy of 53.3%, lower than our interreviewer consistency of 56.1%.

claim: The authors conclude that the limitations of LLM auto-evaluation raise concerns about trusting conclusions based primarily on LLM evaluators.
quote: These limitations of LLM auto-evaluation not only constrain the effectiveness of our over-generate-and-rank paradigm for idea generation but also raise concerns about trusting conclusions that are based primarily on LLM evaluators.

claim: After execution, review scores of LLM-generated ideas fell significantly more than those of expert-written ideas on novelty, excitement, effectiveness and overall (p<0.05), erasing the LLM advantage seen at the ideation stage.
quote: the scores of the LLM-generated ideas decrease significantly more than expert-written ideas on all evaluation metrics (novelty, excitement, effectiveness, and overall; p<0.05), closing the gap between LLM and human ideas observed at the ideation stage.

claim: The study recruited 43 expert researchers to execute randomly assigned ideas (expert-written or LLM-generated); each spent over 100 hours and wrote a 4-page paper on the results.
quote: we conduct an execution study by recruiting 43 expert researchers to execute randomly-assigned ideas, either written by experts or generated by an LLM. Each expert spent over 100 hours implementing the idea and wrote a 4-page short paper to document the experiments.

claim: Executed projects were blindly reviewed by 58 expert reviewers who wrote 181 reviews, so each project received 4-5 reviews.
quote: For the review task, we recruited 58 highly qualified reviewers who collectively wrote 181 reviews, ensuring each project is reviewed by 4-5 different reviewers.

claim: On a 1-10 scale, human ideas kept almost the same novelty, excitement and effectiveness scores after execution (−0.010, +0.078, −0.052), whereas AI ideas dropped by 1.049, 1.760 and 1.879.
quote: human ideas mostly retain the same novelty, excitement, and effectiveness scores after execution (−0.010, +0.078, and −0.052) while AI ideas’ scores decrease by 1.049, 1.760, and 1.879 after execution, on a 1-10 scale.

claim: After execution the ranking flipped, with AI ideas scoring below human ideas on all metrics (e.g., excitement 3.90 vs 4.48, effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78), although these post-execution differences were not statistically significant.
quote: In fact, we see a case where the rankings flip, and AI ideas score below human ideas after execution on all metrics (e.g., 3.90 v.s. 4.48 on excitement and 4.13 v.s. 4.78 on effectiveness). However, we note that such differences are not statistically significant

claim: Ideation-stage review scores were only weakly correlated with post-execution scores in most cases, and for AI ideas the excitement score was even moderately negatively correlated, so ideas judged better before execution did not reliably turn out better.
quote: We further compute the correlation between the ideation scores and execution scores in Appendix D, where the correlation is weak in most cases; and for AI ideas, there is even a moderately negative correlation on the excitement score.

claim: The gap arises partly because execution-stage reviewers consider more factors and ground judgments in actual experiments (empirical performance, rigor, baselines), uncovering weaknesses overlooked when judging ideas alone.
quote: the reviewers are considering more factors during the execution evaluation and grounding their judgment on the executed experiments, therefore uncovering more weaknesses of the ideas that were previously overlooked during ideation evaluation.

claim: The authors acknowledge that 43 executed projects is a modest sample: enough to detect differences in ideation-execution gaps but with reduced power for more granular analyses.
quote: our final sample size of N =43 executed projects remains modest. While sufficient for detecting meaningful differences in the ideation-execution gaps, the sample size may reduce statistical power for other more granular analyses.
